title: How political is your teaching?
author: Murray Sutcliffe
summary: Murray Sutcliffe, an English teacher, opens with a memory of being forbidden to walk across a patch of grass at school and uses it to examine how his own educational beliefs formed in reaction to traditional authority. He admits that embracing inquiry, student agency and critical thinking was partly convenient, since it softened his sense of being less well read than his colleagues. Prompted by Ian Leslie's essay on why the left is bad at education, he starts to see that the values he took for neutral good practice also carry political and philosophical commitments. He traces inquiry and problem-posing education to Dewey's democratic aims and Freire's critique of banking education. He does not abandon his principles but concludes that the questions of what education reflects his values and what actually helps students learn are different, and that he had been quicker to question inherited ideas than the ones he chose.
points: Sutcliffe admits his enthusiasm for inquiry and critical thinking was partly convenient, because it made his lack of literary knowledge less relevant when he joined better-read departments.
Words like critical thinking, agency and equity acquire moral immunity in education, so questioning them sounds absurd and their political origins go unexamined.
Tracing inquiry learning back to Dewey and Freire shows these practices rest on broader views of democracy, freedom and power rather than on evidence alone.
The essay separates two questions that teachers routinely conflate: which education reflects my values, and which teaching actually helps students learn.
He keeps his principles but resolves to apply the same scepticism to the ideas he chose as to the traditions he rejected.
quotes: I wanted to create the type of students who would ask ‘why’ in the face of tradition; the ones who might - metaphorically at least - walk across the grass.
This story appealed to me for a number of reasons, but there is one reason in particular that I have always had a hard time admitting: it was convenient.

So it was awfully convenient for me when I realised that the education tides had been turning, and increasingly foregrounded inquiry-based, student-focused learning and critical thinking. Suddenly my lack of literary knowledge became a little less relevant.

I think every profession has words that acquire a kind of moral immunity. In education, perhaps critical thinking, agency, creativity and equity are among them. To question their value can sound almost absurd.

Perhaps there is no politically neutral way to decide what education should look like. Put thirty children in a room with an adult and you immediately have questions of authority, knowledge, freedom, equality and responsibility.

Paulo Freire took the relationship between pedagogy and politics further. He is critical of what he calls the “banking” concept of education, in which students become passive receptacles to be “filled” by the teacher.

When we say we want students to become independent, critical thinkers, we aren’t just making a claim about what students should learn. When you really think about it, we’re also making a claim about the kinds of people we hope they become.
I became very good at questioning these ideas I’d inherited. I was just less inclined to question the ones I’d chosen to replace them with.
